T1: WRITE(A)
T2: READ(A)
T2: WRITE(A)

Step 1: Identify conflicts.

  • WRITE1(A) occurs before READ2(A).
  • WRITE1(A) occurs before WRITE2(A).
  • READ1(A) occurs before WRITE2(A).

All these conflicts imply

T1​→T2​

Step 2: Construct the graph.

The graph contains an edge from T1 to T2 and no cycle.

Step 3: Conclusion.

The graph is acyclic, so the schedule is conflict-serializable.

Its equivalent serial order is

T1​→T2​​

Solved example: non-conflict-serializable schedule

Consider

S2

Schedule
T1: READ(A)
T2: WRITE(A)
T2: READ(B)
T1: WRITE(B)

Conflicts on A

READ1(A) occurs before WRITE2(A).

Therefore

T1​→T2​

Conflicts on B

READ2(B) occurs before WRITE1(B).

Therefore

T2​→T1​

The precedence graph is

Cycle: T1 → T2 → T1

Because the graph contains a cycle, the schedule is not conflict-serializable.

There is no serial ordering that preserves all conflicting operation orders.

View Serializability

A schedule is view-serializable if it is view-equivalent to some serial schedule.

Two schedules are view-equivalent when they preserve the following three conditions.

Conditions for view equivalence

  1. Initial reads: If a transaction reads the initial value of a data item in one schedule, it must read the initial value of that item in the other schedule as well.
  2. Read-from relationship: If a transaction reads a value written by another transaction, it must read the value written by the same transaction in both schedules.
  3. Final write: The transaction performing the final write on each data item must be the same in both schedules.

These conditions preserve the important read and final-write relationships even when the schedules cannot be transformed into each other by swapping non-conflicting operations.

Example

Consider

S

Schedule
T1: WRITE(A)
T2: WRITE(A)
T1: WRITE(A)

Assume A initially has value A0​.

This schedule has no read operations, so the initial-read and read-from conditions are satisfied vacuously.

The final write on A is performed by T1.

Now consider the serial schedule

S'

Schedule
T2: WRITE(A)
T1: WRITE(A)

The final write on A is also performed by T1, and there are no read relationships to violate.

Therefore, S and S' are view-equivalent, so S is view-serializable.

However, S contains conflicting writes in the order:

  • T1 before T2, giving T1​→T2​.
  • T2 before the final T1 write, giving T2​→T1​.

The precedence graph contains a cycle. Therefore, S is not conflict-serializable.

This demonstrates an important relationship

Conflict serializable⇒View serializable​

But the reverse is not always true.

Conflict vs. view serializability

Conflict serializabilityView serializability
Based on the order of conflicting operation pairs.Based on initial reads, read-from relationships, and final writes.
Tested using a precedence graph.Tested by comparing view-equivalence conditions.
Every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable.Some view-serializable schedules are not conflict-serializable.
Generally easier to test.More difficult to test in the general case.
Does not accept cyclic precedence graphs.Can accept some schedules with cyclic precedence graphs, such as certain blind-write schedules.

A blind write occurs when a transaction writes a data item without first reading that item.

Recoverable, Cascadeless & Strict Schedules

Recoverability of Schedules

Serializability ensures that a schedule is equivalent to a serial execution.

Recoverability concerns whether transactions can commit safely when they depend on values written by other transactions.

To understand recoverability, consider a transaction T2 that reads a value written by T1 before T1 commits.

Schedule
T1: WRITE(A)
T2: READ(A)
T2: COMMIT
T1: COMMIT

T2 reads a value written by T1. If T1 later aborts, T2 has already committed based on invalid data. This is a recovery problem.

Recoverable Schedule

A schedule is recoverable if a transaction commits only after all transactions from which it has read data have committed.

If T2 reads a value written by T1, then T2 must not commit before T1 commits.

Formally, if T2 reads a value of A written by T1, then:

C1​<C2​

Here, Ci​ denotes the commit operation of transaction Ti​.

Example of a recoverable schedule

Schedule
T1: WRITE(A)
T2: READ(A)
T1: COMMIT
T2: COMMIT

Explanation

  1. T1 writes A.
  2. T2 reads the value written by T1.
  3. T1 commits first.
  4. T2 commits afterward.

If T1 commits successfully, T2 can safely commit with respect to this dependency.

Therefore, the schedule is recoverable.

Example of a non-recoverable schedule

Schedule
T1: WRITE(A)
T2: READ(A)
T2: COMMIT
T1: ABORT

Explanation

  1. T1 writes A but has not committed.
  2. T2 reads the uncommitted value written by T1.
  3. T2 commits.
  4. T1 aborts.

T2 has already committed based on a value that was subsequently undone. This schedule is non-recoverable.

Important

A recoverable schedule can still permit dirty reads and cascading rollbacks. Recoverability alone does not prevent these problems.

Cascadeless Schedule

A schedule is cascadeless if a transaction reads a data item only after the transaction that last wrote that value has committed.

In other words, a transaction must not read uncommitted data written by another transaction.

Example of a cascadeless schedule

Schedule
T1: WRITE(A)
T1: COMMIT
T2: READ(A)
T2: COMMIT

Here, T2 reads A only after T1 commits.

Therefore, the schedule is cascadeless.

Example of a schedule that is not cascadeless

Schedule
T1: WRITE(A)
T2: READ(A)
T1: COMMIT
T2: COMMIT

T2 reads A before T1 commits. Therefore, the schedule is not cascadeless, even though it is recoverable.

Advantages of cascadeless schedules

  • Prevents dirty reads.
  • Avoids cascading rollbacks caused by transactions reading uncommitted values.
  • Simplifies transaction recovery.

Strict Schedule

A schedule is strict if, after a transaction writes a data item, no other transaction can read or write that item until the writing transaction commits or aborts.

Thus, a strict schedule prevents other transactions from accessing data written by an uncommitted transaction.

Example of a strict schedule

Schedule
T1: WRITE(A)
T1: COMMIT
T2: READ(A)
T2: WRITE(A)
T2: COMMIT

T2 accesses A only after T1 completes.

Therefore, the schedule is strict.

Example of a schedule that is not strict

Schedule
T1: WRITE(A)
T2: READ(A)
T1: COMMIT
T2: COMMIT

T2 reads A before T1 commits. Hence, the schedule is not strict.

Another violation would be T2 writing A before T1 commits or aborts.

Advantages of strict schedules

  1. Prevents dirty reads and dirty writes.
  2. Simplifies recovery because transactions cannot overwrite or read uncommitted writes from other transactions.
  3. Prevents cascading rollbacks.
  4. Is widely supported through strict locking protocols.

Relationship Between Recoverable, Cascadeless, and Strict Schedules

These three concepts are frequently asked together in DBMS examinations.

The relationship is

Strict Schedules

Cascadeless Schedules

Recoverable Schedules

Every strict schedule is cascadeless, and every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.

Mathematically

Strict⊆Cascadeless⊆Recoverable​

The reverse implications do not necessarily hold.

Comparison table

PropertyRecoverableCascadelessStrict
Reads uncommitted dataMay allowNot allowedNot allowed
Writes an item while another transaction has an uncommitted write on itMay allowMay allowNot allowed
Prevents cascading rollbacksNot necessarilyYesYes
Guarantees recoverabilityYesYesYes
Recovery complexityHigherLowerGenerally simplest

Complete Comparison of Schedule Types

Schedule typeMain criterionHow to identify it
SerialNo interleavingOne transaction finishes before another starts.
Non-serialInterleaving permittedOperations of different transactions are interleaved.
Conflict-serializableConflict-equivalent to a serial schedulePrecedence graph is acyclic.
View-serializableView-equivalent to a serial scheduleInitial reads, read-from relationships, and final writes are preserved.
RecoverableCommit order respects read dependenciesA reader cannot commit before the transaction whose value it read.
CascadelessNo dirty readsTransactions read values only after their writers commit.
StrictNo reads or writes of an item while its previous writer is uncommittedAccess to that item waits until the writer commits or aborts.

Concurrency Control Techniques

Concurrent Transactions

A DBMS may execute several transactions at the same time. This is called concurrent execution.

For example

  • T1 updates Account A.
  • T2 reads Account A.
  • Both transactions execute during overlapping time intervals.

Concurrency improves throughput and resource utilization, but uncontrolled execution can cause problems.

Common concurrency problems

ProblemMeaning
Lost UpdateOne transaction overwrites another transaction's update.
Dirty ReadA transaction reads changes made by another transaction that has not committed.
Non-repeatable ReadRe-reading a row returns a different value because another transaction changed and committed it.
Phantom ReadRepeating a query returns a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows.
Incorrect SummaryAn aggregate calculation observes inconsistent values while another transaction is updating data.

These problems are managed through concurrency-control techniques such as locking, timestamp ordering, and multiversion concurrency control (MVCC).

Concurrency-Control Techniques in DBMS

What is Concurrency Control?

Concurrency control is a mechanism in DBMS that manages the simultaneous execution of multiple transactions to ensure database consistency and correctness.

When multiple transactions access or modify the same data at the same time, incorrect results may occur. Concurrency control prevents or manages these problems.

Example

Suppose an account has a balance of ₹1,000, and two transactions withdraw ₹100 and ₹200 simultaneously.

StepTransaction T1Transaction T2
1Reads ₹1,000
2Reads ₹1,000
3Calculates ₹900
4Calculates ₹800
5Writes ₹900
6Writes ₹800

The final balance becomes ₹800, whereas the correct balance should be ₹700.

This is a Lost Update Problem because T2 overwrites the update performed by T1.

Concurrency-control techniques help prevent such incorrect results.

Objectives of Concurrency Control

  1. Maintain database consistency and integrity.
  2. Prevent lost updates, dirty reads, and other concurrency anomalies.
  3. Ensure serializability whenever required by the chosen correctness guarantees.
  4. Maintain isolation between concurrent transactions.
  5. Maximize concurrency and system throughput without compromising correctness.
  6. Ensure safe transaction execution and recovery.

Classification of Concurrency-Control Techniques

The major techniques are

Lock-Based Concurrency Control

A lock is a mechanism that restricts access to a data item while a transaction is using it.

Before reading or writing a data item, a transaction may need to acquire an appropriate lock.

Types of Locks

There are two basic types of locks.

A. Shared Lock (S-Lock)

A shared lock is used when a transaction wants to read a data item.

  • Multiple transactions can hold shared locks on the same item simultaneously.
  • A transaction holding a shared lock cannot modify the item unless it obtains the required exclusive access.

Example

Schedule
T1: LOCK-S(A)
T1: READ(A)

T2: LOCK-S(A)
T2: READ(A)

Both transactions can read A simultaneously.

B. Exclusive Lock (X-Lock)

An exclusive lock is used when a transaction wants to write or modify a data item.

  • Only one transaction can hold an exclusive lock on an item at a time.
  • Other transactions cannot acquire shared or exclusive locks on that item while the exclusive lock is held.

Example

Schedule
T1: LOCK-X(A)
T1: READ(A)
T1: WRITE(A)
T1: UNLOCK(A)

While T1 holds the exclusive lock, another transaction cannot read or write A using a conflicting lock.

Lock Compatibility Matrix

The following matrix shows whether two lock requests can be granted on the same data item.

Existing lockRequested S-LockRequested X-Lock
S-LockCompatibleNot compatible
X-LockNot compatibleNot compatible
Remember

Shared–shared locks are compatible; all combinations involving an exclusive lock are incompatible.

Two-Phase Locking (2PL)

Two-Phase Locking (2PL) is a locking protocol that ensures conflict serializability when transactions follow its rules.

Each transaction has two phases.

Growing Phase

A transaction can acquire locks and upgrade locks, but cannot release any lock.

Shrinking Phase

A transaction can release locks and downgrade locks, but cannot acquire new locks.

The point at which a transaction obtains its final lock is called the lock point.

Example of 2PL

T1

Schedule
LOCK-X(A)
LOCK-X(B)      -- Growing phase

WRITE(A)
WRITE(B)

UNLOCK(A)
UNLOCK(B)      -- Shrinking phase

Once T1 releases its first lock, it cannot acquire any new lock.

Advantages

  • Ensures conflict serializability.
  • Prevents certain concurrency anomalies.

Disadvantages

  • Can cause deadlocks.
  • Basic 2PL does not necessarily prevent cascading rollbacks.

Variants of Two-Phase Locking

VariantDescriptionMain advantage
Basic 2PLFollows growing and shrinking phases.Ensures conflict serializability.
Conservative 2PLAcquires all required locks before execution.Prevents deadlocks caused by lock waiting.
Strict 2PLHolds exclusive locks until commit or abort.Prevents other transactions from reading or overwriting uncommitted writes.
Rigorous 2PLHolds both shared and exclusive locks until commit or abort.Provides stronger locking discipline and simplifies recovery.

Note that conservative 2PL may reduce concurrency because a transaction must obtain all required locks before starting its work.

Deadlock in Lock-Based Protocols

A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions wait indefinitely for locks held by one another.

Example

T1 holds lock on A and waits for B.

T2 holds lock on B and waits for A.

Neither transaction can proceed.

Common deadlock-handling techniques include

  • Prevention: Design the protocol to prevent circular waiting.
  • Avoidance: Grant requests only when the resulting state is safe, where supported.
  • Detection and recovery: Detect cycles in a wait-for graph and abort a transaction to break the deadlock.
  • Timeout: Abort a transaction if it waits too long, although this can also abort transactions that are not deadlocked.

Timestamp-Based Concurrency Control

Timestamp-based concurrency control assigns a unique timestamp to each transaction and uses these timestamps to determine the permitted order of operations.

A transaction with an earlier timestamp is considered older than one with a later timestamp.

For example

TS(T1) = 10

TS(T2) = 20

Therefore, T1 is older than T2.

For each data item X, the basic timestamp-ordering protocol maintains:

  • Read_TS(X): The largest timestamp of a transaction that has successfully read X.
  • Write_TS(X): The largest timestamp of a transaction that has successfully written X.

Rules of Timestamp Ordering

Rule 1: Read operation READ(X)

When transaction T wants to read X:

  • If TS(T) < Write_TS(X), the read violates the timestamp order, so T is aborted and restarted.
  • Otherwise, the read is allowed, and Read_TS(X) is updated if necessary.

Rule 2: Write operation WRITE(X)

When transaction T wants to write X:

  • If TS(T) < Read_TS(X), the write is rejected because a newer transaction has already read X.
  • If TS(T) < Write_TS(X), the write is rejected under basic timestamp ordering because a newer transaction has already written X.
  • Otherwise, the write is allowed, and Write_TS(X) is updated.

Some systems use variants such as Thomas's Write Rule, which may ignore certain obsolete writes rather than aborting the transaction.

Example

Suppose

TS(T1) = 5

TS(T2) = 10

T2 writes X first, so

Write_TS(X) = 10

Later, T1 tries to write X.

Since

TS(T1) < Write_TS(X)

5 < 10

T1 is aborted under basic timestamp ordering.

Advantages

  • Does not require conventional locks.
  • Transactions follow a timestamp-defined order.
  • Basic timestamp ordering does not cause lock-based deadlocks.

Disadvantages

  • Transactions may be repeatedly aborted and restarted.
  • Starvation can occur.
  • Basic timestamp ordering alone does not guarantee strict, recoverable execution; additional rules may be needed.

What is Thomas Write Rule?

Thomas Write Rule is a modification of the basic Timestamp Ordering Protocol in DBMS that improves concurrency by ignoring certain obsolete write operations instead of rejecting the entire transaction.

Main idea: If a write operation is outdated because a newer value has already been written, the DBMS can ignore that write instead of aborting the transaction.

Rules of Thomas Write Rule

When transaction T executes WRITE(X), the DBMS checks the following conditions in order.

Rule 1

Check whether the write is obsolete

If

TS(T)<Write_TS(X)

the write operation is outdated and is ignored. The transaction is not aborted just because of this write.

Rule 2

Check whether the write violates the read order

Otherwise, if

TS(T)<Read_TS(X)

the transaction is aborted and rolled back, because a newer transaction has already read the value of X.

Rule 3

Perform the write

If neither condition holds, the write is allowed:

X←value

Update

Write_TS(X)=TS(T)

Important

Rule 1 is checked first. If a write is obsolete, it is ignored even if you might otherwise consider the read timestamp condition.

Example of Thomas Write Rule

Consider two transactions

TS(T1​)=5,TS(T2​)=10

Initially

X=100,Write_TS(X)=0,Read_TS(X)=0

Suppose the operations occur in this order:

StepOperationExplanation
1T2​:WRITE(X=200)Allowed. Set Write_TS(X)=10.
2T1​:WRITE(X=150)Since 5<10, this write is obsolete and ignored.
3Final value of XX=200

The older transaction T1​ attempts to overwrite a value already written by the newer transaction T2​.

Thomas Write Rule ignores the outdated write rather than aborting T1​.

Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)

Optimistic concurrency control assumes that conflicts between transactions are relatively infrequent.

Instead of locking every data item throughout execution, a transaction executes first and is checked for conflicts before its updates are committed.

It is commonly described using three phases.

1. Read Phase

Read data and perform calculations using a private workspace.

2. Validation Phase

Check whether committing the transaction would violate the protocol's correctness rules.

3. Write Phase

Apply updates if validation succeeds; otherwise, abort and retry.

Example

Suppose T1 reads an employee's salary and calculates a new value.

  1. T1 reads the salary without holding a long-duration write lock.
  2. T1 calculates the updated salary in its private workspace.
  3. Before committing, the DBMS validates T1 against concurrent transactions.
  4. If validation succeeds, T1 writes the changes.
  5. If validation fails, T1 is aborted and may be restarted.

Advantages

  • Avoids long-duration locks during the read and calculation phases.
  • Works well when conflicts are infrequent.
  • Can provide good performance for read-heavy workloads.

Disadvantages

  • Repeated validation failures can waste computation.
  • May perform poorly when many transactions modify the same data.
  • Validation and retry logic can be complex.

Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC)

Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC) maintains multiple versions of a data item rather than replacing every old value immediately.

Transactions can read an appropriate version of a row based on their snapshot or visibility rules, while other transactions create newer versions.

Example

Suppose a bank account has these versions:

VersionBalance
V1₹1,000
V2₹900
V3₹700

A transaction that started with a snapshot where V1 was visible may continue to read ₹1,000, while a newer transaction may see V3, depending on the database's isolation and visibility rules.

The older version is retained as long as it may be needed by active transactions.

How MVCC works

  1. A transaction starts and obtains the relevant snapshot or visibility context.
  2. Read operations access versions visible to that transaction.
  3. Write operations create or update versions according to the DBMS's implementation.
  4. The DBMS resolves conflicting writes according to its concurrency-control and isolation rules.
  5. Obsolete versions are eventually cleaned up when they are no longer needed.

Advantages

  • Readers can often proceed without blocking writers.
  • Improves performance for read-heavy applications.
  • Supports snapshot-based isolation.

Disadvantages

  • Requires additional storage for multiple versions.
  • Old versions need cleanup.
  • Write conflicts can still occur.
  • Snapshot isolation does not always guarantee full serializability.

MVCC is used by database systems such as PostgreSQL and MySQL's InnoDB engine, although their implementations and isolation semantics differ.

Graph-Based Concurrency-Control Protocols

Graph-based protocols impose an ordering on data items to help ensure serializable execution.

A well-known example is the Tree Protocol.

Under the tree protocol

  1. The first lock may be acquired on any node.
  2. A transaction can lock a node only if it currently holds a lock on that node's parent, except for the first lock.
  3. A transaction can unlock a node at any time.
  4. Once a node is unlocked, that transaction cannot lock it again.

Example

Consider this tree

A transaction can lock A and then B, followed by D.

It cannot lock D first and then lock B afterward, because B is D's parent and the protocol requires the parent to be locked first.

Advantages

  • Ensures conflict serializability.
  • Is deadlock-free under the tree protocol.
  • Allows some locks to be released earlier than under 2PL.

Disadvantages

  • Requires a predefined hierarchy of data items.
  • May impose unnecessary restrictions on access patterns.

Comparison of Concurrency-Control Techniques

TechniqueMain principleDeadlock possibilitySuitable situation
Lock-basedControl access using locksYes, depending on protocolHigh-contention workloads
Timestamp-basedEnforce timestamp orderNo lock-based deadlock in basic protocolWorkloads suited to timestamp ordering
OptimisticValidate before committingNo conventional lock deadlock during its read phaseLow-contention workloads
MVCCMaintain multiple versionsDepends on implementation and additional lockingRead-heavy workloads
Graph-basedEnforce data-item orderingNo deadlock under the tree protocolHierarchical data-access patterns

Recovery & Transaction Commands

Recovery and Transactions

Database recovery ensures that transaction properties are preserved after failures.

Common techniques include

  • Log-based recovery: Records transaction operations or changes in a log.
  • Write-Ahead Logging (WAL): Requires relevant log records to be made durable before corresponding data pages are written.
  • Checkpointing: Records a recovery point to reduce recovery work.
  • Undo: Reverses changes from transactions that must not take effect.
  • Redo: Reapplies changes needed to restore committed work.

For example, if a system crashes after a transaction commits but before every modified data page is written to disk, recovery can use the log to restore the committed result.

Important SQL Transaction Commands

The exact syntax depends on the database system.

SQL
-- Start a transaction
BEGIN;

-- Modify data
UPDATE Employee
SET salary = salary + 1000
WHERE employee_id = 101;

-- Save the changes
COMMIT;

To undo uncommitted changes

SQL
BEGIN;

DELETE FROM Employee
WHERE employee_id = 101;

ROLLBACK;

Some DBMSs also support savepoints, which allow partial rollback within a transaction.

SQL
BEGIN;

UPDATE Account
SET balance = balance - 500
WHERE account_id = 'A';

SAVEPOINT sp1;

UPDATE Account
SET balance = balance + 500
WHERE account_id = 'B';

ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;

COMMIT;

Here, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1 undoes the changes made after the savepoint while keeping earlier changes in the transaction. The final COMMIT commits whatever changes remain.

Normalization & Functional Dependencies

Introduction to Normalization

Normalization is the process of organizing data in a relational database to reduce data redundancy, eliminate insertion, deletion, and update anomalies, and improve data integrity.

It involves dividing a large table into smaller, logically related tables and establishing relationships between them using keys.

Why is normalization needed?

Consider the following table

Student_IDStudent_NameDept_IDDept_Name
101AmanD1CSE
102RaviD1CSE
103PriyaD2ECE
104NehaD1CSE

Problems with this table

  • Data redundancy: The department name CSE is stored multiple times.
  • Update anomaly: If the department name changes, multiple rows must be updated.
  • Insertion anomaly: A new department cannot be stored easily unless a student is assigned to it.
  • Deletion anomaly: Deleting the last student belonging to a department may also remove the only record of that department.

Normalization addresses these problems by separating student and department information.

Anomalies in DBMS

Anomalies are problems that arise when redundant data is stored in an improperly designed database table.

There are three major types.

Insertion Anomaly

An insertion anomaly occurs when we cannot insert certain information into a table without inserting some unrelated information as well.

Example

Suppose we want to add a new department, D3 — Mechanical, but no student has enrolled in it.

If the table requires a student record to store department information, we cannot insert the department independently.

Solution: Store department information in a separate table.

Update Anomaly

An update anomaly occurs when the same information is stored in multiple rows and must be updated in every occurrence.

Example

If the department name changes from CSE to Computer Science, all rows containing CSE must be updated.

If even one row is missed, inconsistent data results.

Solution: Store the department name once in a separate department table.

Deletion Anomaly

A deletion anomaly occurs when deleting one record unintentionally removes other useful information.

Example

Suppose student 104 is the only student in department D2. If we delete that student's row, we may also lose the only stored information about department D2.

Solution: Maintain department information independently of student records.

Functional Dependency (FD)

A functional dependency describes a relationship between attributes in a relation.

If attribute X uniquely determines attribute Y, we write:

X→Y

Here

  • X is called the determinant.
  • Y is the attribute functionally dependent on X.

In simple words, if two rows have the same value of X, they must have the same value of Y.

Example

Consider the relation

STUDENT(Student_ID, Student_Name, Dept_ID)

Student_IDStudent_NameDept_ID
101AmanD1
102RaviD1
103PriyaD2

The following functional dependencies hold, assuming each student ID identifies exactly one student:

Student_ID→Student_Name

Student_ID→Dept_ID

However

Dept_ID→Student_Name

because multiple students can belong to the same department.

Types of functional dependencies

Trivial Functional Dependency

A functional dependency X→Y is trivial if:

Y⊆X

Example

(Student_ID,Student_Name)→Student_Name

It is trivial because Student_Name is already part of the left-hand side.

Non-Trivial Functional Dependency

A functional dependency X→Y is non-trivial if:

Y⊈X

Example

Student_ID→Student_Name

Here, Student_Name is not part of the left-hand side.

Full Functional Dependency

An attribute is fully functionally dependent on a composite determinant if the entire determinant is necessary to determine it.

Example

Consider

ENROLLMENT(Student_ID, Course_ID, Grade)

(Student_ID,Course_ID)→Grade

Assuming a student receives one grade per course, neither Student_ID nor Course_ID alone determines the grade. The complete combination is required.

Partial Functional Dependency

A partial dependency occurs when a non-prime attribute depends on only a proper subset of a composite candidate key.

Consider

ENROLLMENT(Student_ID, Course_ID, Student_Name, Grade)

Candidate key

(Student_ID,Course_ID)

Dependencies

Student_ID→Student_Name

(Student_ID,Course_ID)→Grade

Student_Name depends only on part of the composite key. Therefore, it is a partial dependency.

Important

Partial dependency is the main issue addressed by Second Normal Form (2NF).

Transitive Dependency

A transitive dependency occurs when an attribute depends on another attribute through an intermediate attribute.

Example

STUDENT(Student_ID, Dept_ID, Dept_Name)

Dependencies

Student_ID→Dept_ID

Dept_ID→Dept_Name

Therefore

Student_ID→Dept_Name

The department name is transitively dependent on the student ID through the department ID.

Important

Transitive dependencies involving non-prime attributes are the primary concern addressed by Third Normal Form (3NF).

Important Terms Before Normal Forms

Super Key

A super key is any set of one or more attributes that uniquely identifies every tuple in a relation.

Example

STUDENT(Student_ID, Email, Student_Name)

Assuming both Student_ID and Email are unique:

  • {Student_ID} is a super key.
  • {Email} is a super key.
  • {Student_ID, Student_Name} is also a super key.

A super key may contain unnecessary attributes.

Candidate Key

A candidate key is a minimal super key. No proper subset of it can uniquely identify every tuple.

Example

If both Student_ID and Email are independently unique, the candidate keys are:

  • {Student_ID}
  • {Email}

But {Student_ID, Student_Name} is not a candidate key because Student_Name is unnecessary.

Prime and Non-Prime Attributes

  • Prime attribute: An attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key.
  • Non-prime attribute: An attribute that does not belong to any candidate key.

Example

ENROLLMENT(Student_ID, Course_ID, Grade)

Candidate key: (Student_ID, Course_ID)

  • Prime attributes: Student_ID, Course_ID
  • Non-prime attribute: Grade

These terms are especially important for understanding 3NF and BCNF.

Normal Forms (1NF to 5NF)

Different Normal Forms

The major normal forms are

1NF

First Normal Form

Each attribute contains a single value; no repeating groups or multivalued cells.

2NF

Second Normal Form

Must be in 1NF and have no partial dependency of non-prime attributes on candidate keys.

3NF

Third Normal Form

Must be in 2NF and satisfy the 3NF functional-dependency condition.

BCNF

Boyce–Codd Normal Form

For every non-trivial functional dependency, the determinant must be a super key.

4NF

Fourth Normal Form

Must be in BCNF and have no non-trivial multivalued dependency unless its determinant is a super key.

5NF

Fifth Normal Form

Eliminates non-trivial join dependencies that are not implied by candidate keys.

First Normal Form (1NF)

A relation is in First Normal Form if every attribute contains a single value from its domain and there are no repeating groups or multivalued cells.

Example: Table not in 1NF

STUDENT(Student_ID, Student_Name, Phone_Numbers)

Student_IDStudent_NamePhone_Numbers
101Aman9876, 8765
102Ravi7654
103Priya6543, 5432

The Phone_Numbers column contains multiple values in some rows. This violates 1NF.

Conversion into 1NF

One approach is to create one row for each phone number.

Student_IDStudent_NamePhone_Number
101Aman9876
101Aman8765
102Ravi7654
103Priya6543
103Priya5432

Now every cell contains a single phone number.

However, the key of this relation may be (Student_ID, Phone_Number), and student names are repeated. This can create redundancy that may be addressed by further normalization.

A better design is to separate student information from phone numbers.

STUDENT

Student_ID (PK)Student_Name
101Aman
102Ravi
103Priya

STUDENT_PHONE

Student_ID (FK)Phone_Number
1019876
1018765
1027654
1036543
1035432

Here, Student_ID references the STUDENT table.

Key points about 1NF

  • Every cell contains one value.
  • No repeating groups or multivalued cells.
  • Rows can be uniquely identified by a key.
  • 1NF does not necessarily eliminate all data redundancy.

Second Normal Form (2NF)

A relation is in Second Normal Form if:

  1. It is already in 1NF.
  2. Every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key.

In simple terms, 2NF eliminates partial dependencies.

A relation with a single-attribute candidate key cannot have a partial dependency on that key because it has no proper non-empty subset.

Example: Table not in 2NF

Consider

ENROLLMENT(Student_ID, Course_ID, Student_Name, Course_Name, Grade)

Student_IDCourse_IDStudent_NameCourse_NameGrade
101C1AmanDBMSA
101C2AmanOSB
102C1RaviDBMSA

Assume a student can enroll in many courses and receives one grade per course.

Candidate key

(Student_ID,Course_ID)

Functional dependencies

Student_ID→Student_Name

Course_ID→Course_Name

(Student_ID,Course_ID)→Grade

Here

  • Student_Name depends only on Student_ID.
  • Course_Name depends only on Course_ID.
  • Grade depends on the complete composite key.

Therefore, Student_Name and Course_Name have partial dependencies. The relation violates 2NF.

Conversion into 2NF

Decompose the original relation into three tables.

STUDENT

Student_ID (PK)Student_Name
101Aman
102Ravi

COURSE

Course_ID (PK)Course_Name
C1DBMS
C2OS

ENROLLMENT

Student_ID (FK)Course_ID (FK)Grade
101C1A
101C2B
102C1A

The candidate key of ENROLLMENT is (Student_ID, Course_ID), and Grade depends on the entire key.

Now all three relations satisfy 2NF, assuming the stated dependencies and keys.

Key points about 2NF

  • Must satisfy 1NF.
  • Eliminates partial functional dependencies.
  • Most relevant when candidate keys contain multiple attributes.
  • A relation in 2NF may still contain transitive dependencies.

Third Normal Form (3NF)

A relation is in Third Normal Form if:

  1. It is already in 2NF.
  2. For every non-trivial functional dependency X→A, at least one of the following is true:
    • X is a super key.
    • A is a prime attribute.

In simple terms, 3NF prevents problematic transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on keys.

Example: Table not in 3NF

Consider

STUDENT(Student_ID, Student_Name, Dept_ID, Dept_Name)

Student_IDStudent_NameDept_IDDept_Name
101AmanD1CSE
102RaviD1CSE
103PriyaD2ECE

Assume

Student_ID→Student_Name,Dept_ID

Dept_ID→Dept_Name

Therefore

Student_ID→Dept_Name

through Dept_ID.

The department name is transitively dependent on the student ID.

The relation is already in 2NF because the candidate key contains only one attribute, but it violates 3NF because Dept_ID is not a super key and Dept_Name is non-prime.

Conversion into 3NF

STUDENT

Student_ID (PK)Student_NameDept_ID (FK)
101AmanD1
102RaviD1
103PriyaD2

DEPARTMENT

Dept_ID (PK)Dept_Name
D1CSE
D2ECE

Now the department name is stored only once in the DEPARTMENT table.

Key points about 3NF

  • Must satisfy 2NF.
  • Eliminates transitive dependencies that violate the 3NF condition.
  • Allows a non-super-key determinant when the dependent attribute is prime.
  • Reduces redundancy and improves data consistency.

Boyce–Codd Normal Form (BCNF)

BCNF is a stricter version of 3NF.

A relation is in BCNF if, for every non-trivial functional dependency:

X→Y

X must be a super key.

In simple terms, every determinant of a non-trivial functional dependency must be a super key.

Difference between 3NF and BCNF

  • 3NF permits a non-super-key determinant if the dependent attribute is prime.
  • BCNF does not permit this exception.

Therefore

BCNF⟹3NF

But

3NF⟹BCNF

Example: A relation in 3NF but not BCNF

Consider

CLASS(Student, Subject, Teacher)

Assume the following business rules

  1. Each student studies a subject with a particular teacher.
  2. Each teacher teaches only one subject.
  3. A subject can be taught by multiple teachers.

Functional dependencies

(Student,Subject)→Teacher

Teacher→Subject

Candidate keys

  • (Student, Subject)
  • (Student, Teacher)

All three attributes are prime because each appears in at least one candidate key.

Consider the dependency

Teacher→Subject

Teacher is not a super key because multiple students can have the same teacher.

However, Subject is prime. Therefore, this dependency satisfies 3NF.

It violates BCNF because Teacher is not a super key.

Conversion into BCNF

Decompose into

TEACHER_SUBJECT

Teacher (PK)Subject
T1DBMS
T2OS

STUDENT_TEACHER

StudentTeacher
AmanT1
RaviT2
PriyaT1

This decomposition removes the dependency violation under the stated assumptions.

Important interview point: BCNF decomposition is not always dependency-preserving. A decomposition may preserve all information through a lossless join but require joins to check some original functional dependencies.

Fourth Normal Form (4NF)

4NF deals with multivalued dependencies, which are different from ordinary functional dependencies.

A relation is in 4NF if, for every non-trivial multivalued dependency:

X↠Y

X is a super key.

What is a multivalued dependency?

A multivalued dependency occurs when one attribute determines a set of values of another attribute independently of the remaining attributes.

Example

Consider

STUDENT_INFO(Student, Hobby, Language)

Suppose students can have multiple hobbies and speak multiple languages, and these two facts are independent.

StudentHobbyLanguage
AmanCricketEnglish
AmanCricketHindi
AmanMusicEnglish
AmanMusicHindi

The dependencies are

Student↠Hobby

Student↠Language

Aman has two hobbies and two languages. The table stores all combinations, creating unnecessary redundancy.

Student is not a super key, so the relation violates 4NF.

Conversion into 4NF

STUDENT_HOBBY

StudentHobby
AmanCricket
AmanMusic

STUDENT_LANGUAGE

StudentLanguage
AmanEnglish
AmanHindi

Now hobbies and languages are stored independently.

Key points about 4NF

  • Must satisfy BCNF.
  • Deals with multivalued dependencies.
  • Eliminates redundancy caused by independent multivalued facts.
  • Is particularly useful when a single entity has multiple independent sets of values.

Fifth Normal Form (5NF)

5NF is also called Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF).

A relation is in 5NF if every non-trivial join dependency is implied by its candidate keys.

In simple terms, 5NF deals with cases where a table can be decomposed into three or more smaller tables and reconstructed through joins without losing or introducing invalid information.

Example

Consider

SUPPLY(Supplier, Part, Project)

Suppose the business rules guarantee that a valid supplier-part-project combination exists exactly when all three pairwise relationships exist:

  • The supplier can supply the part.
  • The supplier works on the project.
  • The part is used in the project.

Under this specific rule, the ternary relation can be represented through three pairwise relations.

SUPPLIER_PART

SupplierPart
S1P1
S1P2

SUPPLIER_PROJECT

SupplierProject
S1J1

PART_PROJECT

PartProject
P1J1
P2J1

Joining these relations reconstructs the original combinations under the stated business rule.

However, without that rule, decomposing a ternary relationship into pairwise tables may create spurious combinations.

Key points about 5NF

  • Must satisfy 4NF.
  • Deals with join dependencies.
  • Prevents redundancy caused by complex relationships.
  • Is less commonly needed in ordinary application schemas than 1NF through BCNF.

Comparison of Normal Forms

Normal FormMain conditionProblem addressed
1NFAtomic attribute values; no repeating groupsMultivalued cells
2NFNo partial dependency of non-prime attributesPartial dependency
3NFFor each non-trivial FD, determinant is a super key or dependent attribute is primeTransitive dependency violations
BCNFEvery determinant of a non-trivial FD is a super keyRemaining FD-based anomalies
4NFEvery non-trivial MVD has a super-key determinantIndependent multivalued facts
5NFEvery non-trivial join dependency is implied by candidate keysJoin dependency anomalies

The normal forms form a hierarchy:

5NF⟹4NF⟹BCNF⟹3NF⟹2NF⟹1NF

A relation satisfying a higher normal form also satisfies the lower normal forms in this hierarchy.

Decomposition & Denormalization

Lossless Decomposition

Decomposition means splitting a relation into two or more smaller relations.

A decomposition is lossless if joining the decomposed relations reconstructs exactly the original relation, without losing valid tuples or introducing spurious(extra/unwanted) tuples.

Example

Original relation

STUDENT(Student_ID, Student_Name, Dept_ID, Dept_Name)

Decompose it into

  • STUDENT(Student_ID, Student_Name, Dept_ID)
  • DEPARTMENT(Dept_ID, Dept_Name)

The tables can be joined using Dept_ID to reconstruct the original information, assuming department IDs uniquely identify departments and the foreign-key relationship is maintained.

Binary lossless-join condition

For a decomposition of relation R into R1​ and R2​, the decomposition is lossless with respect to functional dependencies F if:

(R1​∩R2​)→R1​

or

(R1​∩R2​)→R2​

holds in F+, the closure of the functional dependencies.

In simpler terms, the common attributes must functionally determine all attributes of at least one of the decomposed relations.

Dependency Preservation

A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the union of functional dependencies on the decomposed relations is equivalent to the original set of functional dependencies F.

A decomposition D = {R1, R2,..., Rn } of R is dependency preserving with respect to a set of functional dependencies F if:

(F1 ∪ F2 ∪...∪ Fn )+ = F+

Consider a relation R→F with some functional dependencies.

If R is decomposed into R1 with FD {f1} and R2​ with FD {f2}, then there are three cases:

  • f 1 ∪ f 2 = F → Dependency preserving
  • f 1 ∪ f 2 ⊂ 𝐹 → Not dependency preserving
  • f 1 ∪ f 2 ⊃ 𝐹 → Not possible

Lossless join vs dependency preservation

Lossless decompositionDependency preservation
Ensures no information is lost through decompositionEnsures constraints can be enforced without joining tables
Concerned with reconstructing the original relationConcerned with enforcing functional dependencies
A key property of a good decompositionAnother key property of a good decomposition

A decomposition can be lossless without being dependency-preserving.

Interview point: A good schema design generally aims for both lossless decomposition and dependency preservation. However, BCNF decomposition may sacrifice dependency preservation, whereas a suitable 3NF synthesis can achieve both losslessness and dependency preservation.

Denormalization

Denormalization is the intentional introduction of redundant data or the combination of normalized tables to improve read performance.

It is sometimes used when joins become expensive for frequently executed queries.

Example

In a normalized schema, a query may join STUDENT and DEPARTMENT to retrieve the department name for every student.

A denormalized reporting table might store Dept_Name directly alongside each student record to avoid that join.

Advantages

  • Can improve read performance for specific workloads.
  • May reduce the number of joins required.
  • Can simplify analytical and reporting queries.

Disadvantages

  • Introduces data redundancy.
  • Can cause insertion, update, and deletion anomalies.
  • Requires additional synchronization and consistency management.

Normalization vs denormalization

NormalizationDenormalization
Reduces redundancyIntentionally introduces redundancy
Improves consistency and integrityCan improve read performance
Often creates more related tablesMay combine tables or duplicate selected values
Useful for transactional data designUseful for performance-driven workloads and reporting

Denormalization should generally be driven by measured performance requirements, not applied automatically.

Disk Storage & Data Access

Disk Storage and Data Access in DBMS

Before understanding indexing, we must understand how a database stores and retrieves data.

Disk structure

A traditional magnetic disk (HDD) consists of platters that rotate around a spindle. Its physical structure is commonly described using tracks and sectors.

  • Platter: A circular disk that stores data.
  • Track: A concentric circular path on a platter.
  • Sector: A subdivision of a track that stores a small amount of data.
  • Block: A unit of data transfer used in disk I/O terminology. In database systems, a block or page is a fixed-size unit of storage.
  • Offset: The position of a byte within a block or record.

Modern DBMSs generally work with logical block addresses and database pages rather than directly calculating track and sector positions.

Important points

  1. Data stored on secondary storage must generally be brought into memory before the CPU can process it.
  2. Database systems transfer data in pages or blocks rather than fetching an arbitrary byte from disk for every operation.
  3. A disk access can be expensive compared with accessing data already present in RAM.
  4. Database performance is therefore strongly influenced by the number of page reads and writes.

How database tables are stored

Consider an Employee table with the following properties:

PropertyValue
Number of records100
Size of each record128 bytes
Block size512 bytes

Step 1: Calculate records per block

Records per block=128512​=4

Step 2: Calculate the number of blocks

Blocks required=4100​=25

Therefore, the table requires 25 blocks, assuming each block contains four complete records and there is no additional storage overhead.

Full table scan

Suppose we want to find an employee whose ID is 75.

Without an index, the DBMS may have to examine the table's data pages one by one.

  • Best case: The record is found on the first page.
  • Worst case: All 25 pages are examined.
  • If every page must be checked, the number of page reads is 25, assuming none is already cached.

This operation is called a full table scan.

A full table scan is not always bad. It can be efficient when the table is small or the query needs a large percentage of its rows. However, it may become expensive for large tables when only a few records are needed.

Indexing in DBMS

What is an index?

An index is an auxiliary data structure that helps a DBMS locate records without scanning every data page.

It generally stores search-key values and references that help locate the corresponding data.

  • Key (e.g., Employee ID) — 10 bytes
  • Record Pointer (points to the actual record on disk) — 6 bytes

Think of an index like the index at the back of a textbook. Instead of reading every page to find a topic, you use the index to jump to the relevant page.

For example

SQL
SELECT *
FROM Employee
WHERE employee_id = 75;

Without a suitable index, the database may perform a full table scan. With an appropriate index, it can search the index and then retrieve the required record or records.

How an index works

Consider this simplified index

Employee IDRecord pointer
10Page 1, record 1
25Page 1, record 4
50Page 2, record 2
75Page 4, record 1

When the DBMS searches for employee ID 75:

  1. It searches the index for key 75.
  2. It obtains the relevant record location or data-page reference.
  3. It accesses the corresponding data page.
  4. It retrieves the record.

The index is typically much smaller than the complete table, so searching it can require substantially fewer page accesses.

Numerical example: Why indexing helps

Continue with the Employee table.

Assume

  • 100 records
  • 25 data blocks
  • 512-byte blocks
  • Each simplified index entry occupies 16 bytes: 10 bytes for the key and 6 bytes for the pointer.

The pointer size and key size here are illustrative, not universal database specifications.

Index entries per block

16512​=32

Index blocks required

⌈32100​⌉=4

For a simple linear scan of this index, followed by one data-page access, the worst-case estimate is:

4+1=5 page reads

This is compared with up to 25 data-page reads for a full table scan.

Advantages of indexing

  • Faster lookups using indexed columns.
  • Faster filtering for suitable WHERE conditions.
  • Improved performance for many joins.
  • Efficient ordering and range queries with suitable indexes.
  • Potentially reduced disk I/O.

Disadvantages of indexing

  • Requires additional storage.
  • Increases the cost of INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations because affected indexes must be maintained.
  • Too many indexes can increase storage and maintenance costs.
  • An index may not be useful when a query retrieves most of the table.
  • Poor index selection can increase rather than reduce query cost.

Main categories of indexes

Indexes can be classified along different, partly independent dimensions.

ClassificationTypesWhat it describes
By organizationClustered, non-clusteredHow the index relates to data storage
By densityDense, sparseHow many search-key entries are maintained
By structureB+ Tree, hash, bitmap, etc.How the index organizes and searches keys
By constraintUnique, non-uniqueWhether duplicate indexed values are permitted
By coverageCovering, non-coveringWhether an index contains everything a query needs
By storage modelRow-oriented, column-orientedHow the underlying table data is stored

These classifications should not be confused. For example, a unique index can also be a B+ Tree index, and a clustered index may have different implementation details in different database systems.

Dense Index and Sparse Index

These two index types are distinguished by the number and placement of index entries.

Dense index

A dense index contains an index entry for every record in the database.

Structure

Each index entry stores

  • Key
  • Pointer to the actual record

Employee records

Employee IDRecord
1Record 1
2Record 2
3Record 3
4Record 4

Dense index

KeyPointer
1Record 1
2Record 2
3Record 3
4Record 4

Advantages

  • Provides a direct route to the matching record or records.
  • Supports fast searches.
  • Does not require searching through an entire data block to locate the indexed key.

Disadvantages

  • Requires more index storage.
  • Increases index maintenance work during data modifications.

Sparse index

A sparse index contains index entries for only some records, not all.

Typically, there is one index entry per block.

Structure

Each index entry stores

  • Key
  • Pointer to a block (not the exact record)

Suppose we search for employee ID 5.

  1. The index shows that block 2 begins with key 4.
  2. The DBMS identifies block 2 as the relevant block.
  3. It searches within that block to find key 5.

Advantages

  • Requires less storage.
  • Has fewer entries to maintain.
  • Can be efficient when data is ordered and blocks contain many records.

Disadvantages

  • May require additional searching within the selected data block.
  • Generally requires an ordered data file or another suitable organization to identify the correct block reliably.

Dense index vs. sparse index

FeatureDense indexSparse index
EntriesEvery search-key value or recordSelected search-key values
StorageHigherLower
SearchMore directMay require a local scan
Underlying data orderDepends on implementationTypically requires ordered data
MaintenanceUsually more entries to updateOften fewer entries to update

Interview point: Sparse indexing works especially well with ordered data. A classic sparse index stores one entry per data block, often pointing to the first key in that block.

Multi-Level Indexing, B Trees & B+ Trees

Multi-Level Indexing

When the table grows (e.g., 1000 rows → 40 index blocks), searching the index itself becomes slow. Solution: add an index on top of the index.

Level 1: Index entries that point to the underlying data blocks or lower-level index pages.

Level 2: Index entries that point to Level 1 pages.

Higher levels: Additional index pages that direct the search toward the appropriate lower level.

Database table: 250 blocks

Level-1 index: 40 blocks

Level-2 index: 2 blocks

Search: 2 blocks (L2) + 1 block (L1) + 1 data block = 4 blocks

Repeatedly building indexes on lower-level indexes creates a hierarchical structure.

When rotated visually, multi-level index looks exactly like a tree — this is the origin of B Trees.

Problem: Managing these index levels manually is impractical. We need self-managing, automatically growing/shrinking multi-level indexes → This motivates balanced tree structures such as B-Trees and B+ Trees.

M-Way Search Trees

An extension of Binary Search Trees (BST) where each node can have M children and M−1 sorted keys.

PropertyBinary search treeM-way search tree
Maximum children2M
Maximum keys per node1M−1
Key orderBased on left/right relationshipsKeys within each node are sorted
Search pathsOne of up to two branchesOne of up to M branches

A binary search tree is the special case M=2.

Node structure (M = 4):

Problem with ordinary M-way search trees

An M-way search tree does not automatically remain balanced.

If insertions create a highly uneven structure, the height may become large, and searches can approach linear time in the number of keys.

The solution is to impose structural constraints. B-Trees and B+ Trees are balanced multiway search trees designed for this purpose.

B Trees

B Trees = M-Way Search Trees with rules to control structure.

A B-Tree is a self-balancing multiway search tree in which keys are maintained in sorted order, all leaves are at the same depth, and insertion or deletion operations preserve the tree's structural rules.

B-Trees are suitable for storage systems because each node can be sized to fit a disk page and contain many keys and child pointers.

Properties of a B-Tree

Using the common definition where the order M is the maximum number of children:

  1. Each node can have at most M children.
  2. Each node can have at most M−1 keys.
  3. Except for the root, each internal node has at least ⌈M/2⌉ children.
  4. A non-root node therefore has at least ⌈M/2⌉−1 keys.
  5. If the root is not a leaf, it has at least two children.
  6. All leaves occur at the same depth.
  7. Keys within each node are sorted.
  8. A B-Tree remains balanced as records are inserted and deleted.
  9. Creation is bottom-up (tree grows upward)

B-Tree node structure

A B-Tree node can contain

  • Sorted keys.
  • Child pointers for navigating to other nodes.
  • Data pointers or record references (— one per key) associated with keys, depending on the implementation.

This means that a search can sometimes finish at an internal node rather than reaching a leaf.

Insertion and splitting

When a node is full and a new key must be inserted, the node may split. A separator key is promoted to the parent so that the search-order property is preserved.

If the root splits, a new root is created, increasing the height by one.

Example using a B-Tree of order 4, with at most three keys per node:

Insert the keys 10, 20, and 40:

10 | 20 | 40

One node has reached its maximum capacity.

Now insert 50. Under the convention that splitting a full node promotes a middle separator, the tree reorganizes so the keys remain ordered and each node respects its capacity. The exact split arrangement depends on the insertion algorithm and overflow convention.

For an overflow of four keys, one possible resulting arrangement is:

Illustrative split for an overflow of four keys; splitting rules vary by convention.

Advantages of B-Trees

  • Balanced height.
  • Efficient exact-key search.
  • Efficient insertions and deletions.
  • Suitable for disk-based storage because nodes can hold multiple keys.
  • Avoids the deep structure that can occur in an ordinary unbalanced search tree.

Key Differences from B Trees

FeatureB TreeB+ Tree
Record pointersEvery node (all keys)Leaf nodes only
Keys in leavesSome keys may only be in internal nodesAll keys must appear in leaf nodes
Leaf connectivityNot connectedLinked list (left to right)
Index typeMixInternal = sparse index, Leaves = dense index

Limitations for database indexing

B-Trees can store records or record pointers in internal nodes as well as leaves. As a result, their leaf nodes do not necessarily contain every search key.

This is not inherently incorrect, but it is less convenient for ordered range scans when compared with a design that stores all entries at the leaf level and links the leaves together.

This leads to the B+ Tree.

B+ Trees

B+ Trees are a modification of B Trees better suited for database indexing.

How B+ Trees Work

  • Internal (non-leaf) nodes store only keys for routing — no record pointers
  • Leaf nodes store all keys + record pointers
  • Any key that appears internally is duplicated at the leaf level
  • All leaves are at the same level and linked together like a linked list

Why B+ Trees Are Better for Databases

Find by ID: Traverse from root → internal nodes → leaf. Always exactly log(n) disk reads (predictable).

Searching in a B+ Tree

Suppose we need to find employee ID 45.

  1. Start at the root.
  2. Compare 45 with the separator keys.
  3. Follow the appropriate child pointer.
  4. Repeat until reaching the leaf page.
  5. Find key 45 in the leaf.
  6. Use its record reference to retrieve the actual row if the leaf does not already contain the row.

The number of page accesses is related to the height of the tree, not the total number of rows scanned sequentially.

Range query (e.g., rows 100–600):

  • Reach the starting leaf via tree traversal
  • Then linearly scan the linked leaf nodes without going back to the root
  • Extremely efficient — leaves are already sorted and connected

Suppose we execute

SQL
SELECT *
FROM Employee
WHERE employee_id BETWEEN 100 AND 600;

A B+ Tree can process the query efficiently:

  1. Search for the first relevant key, 100.
  2. Locate its leaf page.
  3. Scan entries in sorted order.
  4. Follow the leaf-level sibling pointers into subsequent pages.
  5. Stop when keys exceed 600.

The typical index traversal cost can be expressed as:

O(logN+K)

Here, N is the number of indexed entries and K is the number of matching entries examined, abstracting away page sizes and output costs.

Insert/Update/Delete

  • Read only the relevant B+ tree nodes (a few disk blocks)
  • Modify in memory, flush back to disk
  • No need to rewrite the entire file
  • Changes are local — other blocks untouched

Why Databases Use B+ Trees (Not B Trees)

B Trees store data in internal nodes too, which means range queries require jumping around the tree. B+ Trees force all data to the leaf level, enabling:

  • Predictable read time for any row
  • Efficient sequential scan for range queries via the leaf linked list

Both SQL (MySQL, PostgreSQL) and NoSQL (MongoDB's WiredTiger engine) use B+ Trees to store table/collection data on disk.

Summary Diagram

Index Types: Clustered & Non-Clustered

Clustered and Non-Clustered Indexes

This classification describes the relationship between the index and the organization of the underlying table.

Clustered index

A clustered index organizes the table's data according to the clustered search key.

When you create a clustered index on a column (e.g., CustomerID), two things happen:

  1. The database physically reorders all the data pages so rows are sorted by that column — lowest to highest.
  2. It builds a B-tree (Balanced Tree) — an upside-down hierarchical structure:
    • Root node — one index page at the top
    • Intermediate nodes — index pages pointing to other index pages
    • Leaf nodes — the actual data pages (physically sorted)

To find a row, the database traverses from root → intermediate → leaf, following pointers. For a 20-row table split across 4 pages, finding row 14 takes just 3 hops (root → intermediate → data page), reading only 1 data page instead of all 4.

Key rules

  • You can only have one clustered index per table — because data can only be physically sorted one way
  • Best column: one that is unique and rarely updated — the primary key is ideal (unique + never changes)
  • Also great for range queries (e.g., WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 50)

Non-clustered index

A non-clustered index is a separate index structure whose leaf entries contain the indexed key and a locator for the corresponding row or clustered key.

A non-clustered index does not touch or reorder the actual data. Instead, it builds a completely separate B-tree structure:

  • Root and intermediate nodes — same as clustered index (index pages pointing to index pages)
  • Leaf nodes — index pages containing row locators (row identifiers, or RIDs), each storing the exact file ID + page number + row offset where the actual row lives in the data pages

The data pages themselves remain in their original heap order and are not part of this B-tree at all.

To find a row, the traversal goes: root → intermediate → leaf (row locator page) → jump to exact row in data page. This is one extra hop compared to a clustered index, making it slightly slower for reads.

Key rules

  • You can create as many as needed — each is a separate B-tree with pointers to the same data
  • Best for columns used in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, or exact-match lookups on non-primary-key columns
  • Writes are faster than with a clustered index, since the physical data pages don't need re-sorting

Tradeoffs at a glance

ClusteredNon-clustered
Max per table1Unlimited
Leaf level containsActual data pagesRow locator pointers
Read speedFasterSlightly slower (extra hop)
Write speedSlower (must re-sort)Faster
StorageMore efficientUses extra space for index pages
Physical data orderChangedUntouched

Database Replication

What is database replication?

Database replication is the process of copying and maintaining the same data across multiple servers so that the system continues to work even if one server goes down.

The result is several live copies of your database running simultaneously.

The main objectives are

  • High availability.
  • Improved read performance.
  • Fault tolerance.
  • Disaster recovery.
  • Reduced latency for users in different geographic regions.

A classic example: an e-commerce site uses one primary database to handle orders (writes), and a fleet of read replicas to serve product listings, search results, and user profiles (reads).

Replication creates multiple copies of data. It does not, by itself, divide the dataset into smaller pieces.

How it works

  1. A primary database is designated as the single source of truth for all changes.
  2. Replica databases are configured to receive data from the primary.
  3. Every insert, update, or delete on the primary is recorded — typically in a transaction log or via change data capture (CDC).
  4. Those captured changes are transmitted to replicas over the network, either instantly or at intervals.
  5. Replicas apply the changes to bring themselves in sync.
  6. The system continuously monitors sync state and handles delays or conflicts.
  7. Applications read from replicas and write to the primary (or in some models, write to any node).

Types of replication

1. Master-slave (primary-replica)

One master handles all writes. Slaves receive a copy and serve reads.

  • Write path: master only
  • Read path: any slave
  • Failure: if the master dies, a slave must be manually or automatically promoted
  • Best for: read-heavy applications — social feeds, product catalogues, CMS

The key limitation is that write capacity doesn't scale — everything still flows through one master. Also introduces replication lag, meaning slaves may be slightly behind the master.

2. Master-master (multi-master)

Two or more nodes each accept reads and writes. Changes on one are synced to the others.

  • All nodes are peers — any can accept a write
  • Requires conflict resolution: if two nodes update the same row simultaneously, the system must decide which wins (last-write-wins, vector clocks, application logic, etc.)
  • Best for: multi-datacenter setups, collaborative platforms, globally distributed writes

More powerful but significantly more complex to manage. A misconfigured conflict resolution strategy can silently corrupt data.

3. Snapshot replication

A full copy of the entire database is taken at a point in time and sent to subscribers.

  • Not real-time — the snapshot represents the state at one moment
  • Simple to set up and restore from
  • Best for: data warehousing, analytics, compliance/auditing, periodic reporting
  • Not suitable where data changes constantly and freshness matters

4. Transactional replication

Every individual transaction (insert/update/delete) is captured and sent to subscribers in near real-time, one change at a time.

  • Maintains high consistency across locations
  • Publisher → distributor → subscriber pipeline
  • Best for: financial systems, live dashboards, online gaming, any scenario requiring fresh data everywhere

Adds some overhead on the publisher and requires careful agent/distributor configuration.

5. Merge replication

Both the publisher and subscribers can modify data independently. Changes are merged during synchronisation, with conflicts detected and resolved.

  • Two-way (bidirectional) sync
  • Works for intermittently connected systems — devices can work offline and sync later
  • Best for: field service apps, healthcare devices, mobile apps that work without connectivity

Conflict resolution here is the hardest problem — the same record might be edited on two devices with no connectivity between them.

Replication configurations (how it's timed)

Synchronous replication

The primary waits for at least one replica to confirm receipt before committing the transaction. This guarantees no data is lost if the primary crashes immediately after a write.

  • Strong consistency
  • Higher latency — every write is slower because it waits
  • Used when data loss is completely unacceptable (banking, payments)

Asynchronous replication

The primary commits immediately and sends changes to replicas in the background. Replicas catch up with a slight delay.

  • Low latency — primary doesn't wait
  • Risk of data loss: if the primary crashes before a replica receives the change, that change is gone
  • Acceptable in most read-heavy web apps where slight lag is tolerable

Semi-synchronous replication

A middle ground: the primary waits for confirmation from at least one replica, then proceeds. Other replicas catch up asynchronously.

  • Balances consistency and performance
  • Ensures at least one copy always has the latest data

Why replication matters in system design

High availability — if the primary goes down, a replica can be promoted to take over. The system keeps running with minimal or zero downtime.

Load balancing — a load balancer can route all read queries to replicas, leaving the primary free to handle writes. This is one of the most common and impactful performance optimisations.

Disaster recovery — geographically separated replicas survive regional outages, data centre fires, or infrastructure failures.

Fault tolerance — individual server failures don't take the system down because traffic shifts to surviving replicas automatically.

Data locality — replicas placed physically close to users in different regions reduce latency for those users significantly.

Scalability — adding more read replicas lets the system handle more concurrent users without touching the primary.

Challenges

Replication lag — in async replication, replicas can be seconds (or more) behind the primary. A user who just wrote data may immediately read a replica and see stale data — a common source of bugs in distributed systems.

Conflict resolution — in multi-master setups, simultaneous writes to the same row on different nodes create conflicts. No universal correct answer — strategy depends on the domain (last-write-wins, application-level logic, manual resolution).

Complexity — setting up and maintaining replication pipelines, monitoring lag, handling failovers, and configuring agents/distributors requires significant expertise.

Write bottleneck — master-slave does nothing for write scalability. If the app is write-heavy, replication alone doesn't help — you need sharding or master-master.

Consistency vs. latency tradeoff — synchronous gives you consistency but costs latency. Async gives you speed but risks lost writes. You cannot fully have both.

Cost — every replica is another server. Large-scale deployments with many replicas across multiple regions are expensive to run and maintain.

Data Partitioning

Data Partitioning

Data partitioning divides a large table or dataset into smaller logical parts called partitions.

Partitioning may occur within one database server or across multiple servers.

The objectives include

  • Better query performance.
  • Partition pruning.
  • Easier maintenance.
  • Improved manageability of large tables.
  • Parallel processing in suitable systems.

There are two main types

  • Horizontal Partitioning → splits data by rows (e.g., users by region)
  • Vertical Partitioning → splits data by columns (e.g., separating personal info from transaction data)

The six partitioning methods

1. Horizontal partitioning

Horizontal Partitioning divides data by rows, but all partitions may still exist on the same server. When these horizontal partitions are placed across multiple servers, the approach is called Sharding.

Each partition contains the same logical columns but a different subset of rows.

Example

Original table

User IDNameRegion
1AshaIndia
2RaviUS
3NehaIndia
4OmarEurope

Possible horizontal partitions

  • Partition 1: users in India.
  • Partition 2: users in the US.
  • Partition 3: users in Europe.

All partitions share the same logical schema.

Advantages

Horizontal partitioning divides a table into multiple parts by distributing rows across different partitions or servers.

• Scalability: Allows parallel processing of large datasets across multiple nodes.

• Load Balancing: Distributes workload evenly, reducing system bottlenecks.

• Fault Tolerance: Each partition works independently, improving reliability during failures.

Disadvantages

Despite its scalability benefits, it introduces some complexity in database operations.

• Complex Joins: Joins across multiple partitions can be slower and harder to manage.

• Data Skew: Uneven data distribution may cause certain partitions to handle more load than others.

Vertical Partitioning

Vertical partitioning divides a table by columns. Each resulting structure contains a subset of the original columns, with a shared identifier or key used to associate related rows.

Example

Original Users table

Users(

Schedule
    user_id,
    name,
    email,
    bio,
    avatar,
    preferences
)

Vertical split

Users_Core(

Schedule
    user_id,
    name,
    email
)
Users_Profile(
    user_id,
    bio,
    avatar,
    preferences
)

The shared user_id connects the two structures.

Good for: tables with many columns where only a subset is frequently accessed; reduces I/O by not reading unused columns

Advantages

Vertical partitioning divides a table by separating columns into different partitions based on usage or functionality.

  • Better Query Performance: Reduces data read by isolating frequently accessed columns.
  • Efficient Retrieval: Fetches only needed columns, saving I/O and storage.
  • Easier Schema Changes: Simplifies adding or removing columns.

Disadvantages

Although useful for column-level optimization, it can introduce additional query complexity.

  • Query Complexity: Queries may need to access multiple partitions.
  • Slower Joins: Combining data from different partitions adds overhead.
  • Limited Scalability: Not ideal for datasets with rapidly growing columns.

3. Key-based Partitioning

Divides data based on a specific key or attribute, with each partition holding all data related to that key. Common in distributed systems for uniform data distribution and efficient key-based lookups.

A hash function on the key determines the destination partition.

Good for: point lookups — "give me all data for user X" is fast because it's all in one partition

Disadvantages

Watch out for: hot keys cause one partition to handle disproportionate load; range queries are inefficient since consecutive keys may scatter across partitions.

4. Range partitioning

Partitions are defined by value ranges — date ranges, ID ranges, alphabetical ranges. A query for data within a range hits only the relevant partition(s).

  • Good for: time-series data, logs, any naturally ordered data; range queries are highly efficient
  • Watch out for: if recent data is queried far more than old data (which is typical), the "current" partition is always hot; requires ongoing maintenance as ranges fill up

5. Hash-based partitioning

A hash function is applied to the data and the output determines which partition it goes to. Similar to key-based but the hash randomises placement rather than grouping by key identity.

  • Good for: even distribution across partitions; write-heavy workloads where you want to spread load uniformly
  • Watch out for: terrible for range queries (consecutive values are randomised across partitions); resharding requires rehashing all data

6. Round-robin partitioning

Records are assigned to partitions in a rotating sequence — record 1 to partition 1, record 2 to partition 2, record 3 to partition 3, record 4 back to partition 1, and so on.

  • Good for: achieving near-perfect write distribution without needing a meaningful key; simple to implement
  • Watch out for: no data locality — related records are spread everywhere; any query that needs to find "all records matching X" must scan all partitions; poor fit for analytical or key-based queries

Partition pruning

Partition pruning occurs when the DBMS determines that some partitions cannot contain rows matching a query and skips them.

Example

SQL
SELECT *
FROM Orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'
  AND order_date <  '2026-02-01';

If the table is partitioned by month, the DBMS may scan only the January 2026 partition.

Pruning depends on the partition definition, the query predicates, and the database optimizer.

Database Sharding

What is sharding?

Database sharding is a horizontal scaling technique where a large dataset is split into smaller chunks called shards, each stored on a multiple database instances.

Every shard holds the same schema as the original database, but each row appears in exactly one shard — there is no duplication of data across shards (unlike replication, which copies everything).

The key idea: instead of one massive database server struggling under load, you spread the data across many smaller servers, each handling only a fraction of the total dataset.

Sharding key

A shard key is the attribute or combination of attributes used to determine where a record is stored.

Examples

  • user_id
  • customer_id
  • order_date
  • (region, customer_id)

A good shard key should distribute data and workload reasonably evenly while supporting common query patterns.

A poor shard key may cause:

  • Uneven storage distribution.
  • Hot partitions.
  • Expensive cross-shard queries.
  • Difficult rebalancing.

Sharding methods

1. Key-based (hash-based) sharding

A hash function is applied to a shard key (e.g., customer_id) to determine which shard stores that row. For example, with 3 shards: shard = customer_id % 3. The remainder (0, 1, or 2) decides the destination.

  • Pros: uniform distribution if the key is well-chosen; consistent placement means you always know where a record lives without a lookup
  • Cons: adding or removing shards requires rehashing everything; hot keys cause uneven load; choosing a bad shard key breaks the uniformity

2. Range-based sharding

Data is divided by value ranges of a column. For example, customers whose names start with A–P go to shard 1, Q–Z to shard 2. Or orders from January–June go to shard 1, July–December to shard 2.

  • Pros: natural fit for time-series or ordered data; range queries are efficient since all matching data is in one shard
  • Cons: uneven distribution if data is skewed toward certain ranges (e.g., most customers have names starting with S); one shard can become a hotspot

3. Directory-based sharding

A central lookup service (a directory or lookup table) maps each shard key to its shard location. Every query first asks the directory which shard to go to, then routes there.

  • Pros: flexible — you can move data between shards without changing application logic; supports dynamic scaling
  • Cons: the directory is a single point of failure; every query incurs an extra network hop to the directory, increasing latency

Sharding vs. partitioning — the distinction

These terms are often used interchangeably, but there is a meaningful difference. Partitioning is the general concept of dividing data — it can happen on a single machine. Sharding is a specific type of horizontal partitioning where each partition lives on a completely separate database server, giving you true distributed scale. All sharding is partitioning, but not all partitioning is sharding.
